name: Ungoogled Chromium
summary: Patch set and build system producing Chromium without its dependency on Google web services, distributed through distribution repositories, Flathub and contributor builds rather than official binaries.
license: BSD 3-Clause (project's own patches and tooling); Chromium source and bundled components under their own licences

content.introduction: ungoogled-chromium is not a browser with its own vision of the web: it is Google Chromium with the Google web-service dependency removed, and its maintainers insist on that framing. The project's first objective is that it is "Google Chromium, sans dependency on Google web services"; the second is that it retains the default Chromium experience as closely as possible, making it essentially a drop-in replacement rather than a redesign; only the third concerns the privacy, control and transparency tweaks it adds, most of which must be enabled manually. The result is a browser that looks and behaves like Chromium — same interface, same extension model, same engine — but which does not phone home, does not use Google's binaries, blocks requests to Google's infrastructure at runtime and disables functionality tied to Google's services, including Safe Browsing. It is distributed as patches and build recipes rather than as a vendor product: the project publishes source and platform-specific build repositories, and the binaries most users install come from their distribution, from Flathub, or from contributors who build and upload them.
content.origin_and_history: The project dates from the middle of the last decade: the public repository was created in June 2015 and by October 2026 it carried more than 2,400 commits, 435 tags and a substantial community, with roughly 28,000 stars and well over a thousand forks reported in repository metadata. Its design inherits from earlier efforts to strip Google integration from Chromium, and the project credits them explicitly: the Inox patchset, Bromite, Debian's Chromium packaging and Iridium Browser are named as sources of borrowed features, in that order of significance. The project has since become an upstream of its own, with forks and downstream projects listed as users of its changes, among them Bromite, which borrows patches, and a ppc64le fork. Development is organised around one common repository plus per-platform repositories — Arch, Debian and Ubuntu, Fedora and CentOS, portable Linux, Windows, macOS, Android — each carrying the configuration and scripts needed to build the browser for that target. The common repository holds the patches, the utilities and the design documentation, and its tags mark the revisions other builds reference.
content.rendering_engine_and_technical_architect: Because it is compiled from Chromium source, ungoogled-chromium runs the same engines as Chromium — Blink for layout and rendering, V8 for JavaScript — and inherits Chromium's multi-process site isolation, sandboxing and GPU architecture. What the project changes is the code that connects the browser to Google's services, and it does so through four mechanisms it documents. First, it removes functionality specific to Google domains: the Google Host Detector, the Google URL Tracker, Google Cloud Messaging and Google Hotwording are named examples, and Safe Browsing is disabled as part of the same policy. Second, it blocks internal requests to Google at runtime as a fail-safe, by replacing many Google domains in the source with non-existent alternatives under the top-level domain `qjz9zk` and then patching the browser to refuse connections to them — the technique called domain substitution. Third, it strips pre-built binaries from the source tree, a step the project calls binary pruning, replacing them with user-provided alternatives where possible. Fourth, it disables features that inhibit control and transparency and adds switches to restore them. The HSTS preload list is explicitly excluded from domain substitution, which the FAQ documents. Everything else — the profile format, extension APIs, renderer sandbox — is Chromium's.
content.interface_and_documented_features: The interface is Chromium's, unchanged by design, and the project's own additions are mostly settings and switches. It adds command-line switches and `chrome://flags` entries to configure new behaviour, all disabled by default, with an exhaustive list published in its documentation. It adds a Suggestions URL field to the search-engine editor at `chrome://settings/searchEngines`, allows more URL schemes to be saved with a page, and adds a "No Search" omnibox provider so that searching can be disabled entirely. It forces all pop-ups into tabs, stops the omnibox from reformatting URLs (for example stripping `http://` or hiding parameters), and disables the intranet redirect detector, which generates extraneous DNS requests — an acknowledged trade-off, since it breaks captive-portal detection although captive portals still work. On Windows, downloaded files no longer receive a Zone Identifier. One default is worth flagging because users notice it immediately: as the FAQ explains, the setting "Delete data sites have saved to your device when you close all windows" is selected by default, so sessions do not survive a restart until the user changes it. The project is explicit that most privacy-related enhancements require manual activation.
content.installation_and_distribution: Distribution is the weakest link in the project and the documentation says so. ungoogled-chromium is available through software repositories maintained by the community for Arch (AUR), Debian and Ubuntu (an openSUSE Build Service repository for Debian, the XtraDeb PPA for Ubuntu), Fedora (a COPR) and derivatives, Gentoo (the `::pf4public` overlay, with both source and binary ebuilds), FreeBSD (pkg) and OpenBSD (ports), with openSUSE packaging under `network:chromium`, and it is the default browser of OpenMandriva. Distribution-independent routes exist through Flathub under the identifier `io.github.ungoogled_software.ungoogled_chromium`, GNU Guix and nixpkgs. On macOS it is installed through the Homebrew cask. Beyond those package sources, the project points to a separate catalogue of contributor binaries with an unusually candid warning: because those binaries are not necessarily reproducible, authenticity cannot be guaranteed and there is always a non-zero probability that they have been tampered with. No official installer, signed release artefact or vendor download page is published by the project itself, which distinguishes it sharply from the other browsers in this library.
content.platforms_and_hardware_architectures: The project documents seven supported targets, each with its own repository: Android, Arch Linux, Debian and Ubuntu with derivatives, Fedora and CentOS, portable Linux for any distribution, Windows, and macOS. That list is the project's own definition of officially supported platforms; other systems are discussed in the issue tracker rather than supported. Architectures are inherited from each platform build rather than declared centrally: the project publishes no architecture matrix, no minimum operating system version, no memory or disk requirement and no processor instruction baseline on the pages consulted, and because the browser is built from Chromium source, practical requirements follow the Chromium release being packaged. On Linux the documented Namespace Sandbox requirement is the kernel option `unprivileged_userns_clone`, which the FAQ presents as the fix when the sandbox does not work — a reminder that the security model is only fully active when the host permits it. Windows-specific documented behaviour includes the Zone Identifier change; macOS and Windows builds otherwise follow Chromium's platform conventions.
content.extensions_and_add_on_store: Extensions are Chromium extensions, but the installation path is not. The FAQ states that extensions and themes from the Chrome Web Store can be installed, though not through the Web Store interface: instead the CRX download URL is used, either directly, as a custom search engine entry, or through a bookmarklet, and the resulting file is installed through the extension MIME handling flag, a `file://` URL, drag and drop, or — on Linux — an external extension descriptor. A third-party extension called chromium-web-store is recommended for anyone who wants installation and updates handled automatically. There is, in the project's words, currently no built-in functionality for extension auto-updates. The FAQ confirms that all plugins work, including PepperFlash and Widevine DRM, and documents the manual installation of the Widevine CDM on Linux, Windows and macOS — with the caveat that the Chrome build used for the component should match the browser's major version to avoid instability. In short, the extension ecosystem is intact but every convenience layer around it has been removed.
content.privacy_and_security_model: The privacy model is subtractive: remove every background request to a Google service, remove the code specific to those services, and block anything that slips through. Domain substitution and the `trk:` scheme block provide the runtime backstop, and the design documentation describes the pipeline that generates the substitution list. Safe Browsing is disabled deliberately; the project's FAQ explains that Safe Browsing communicates with Google servers to download blocklists and recommends uBlock Origin or uMatrix to anyone who wants comparable protection, which means the browser ships without phishing and malware warnings. The browser keeps Chromium's sandbox, site isolation and renderer model — including the Linux namespace sandbox with its documented kernel prerequisite — and the project does not claim any additional hardening of memory safety or exploit mitigations. Its security posture therefore differs from stock Chromium mainly in what is absent: Google's update and service channels, Google's binaries, and Safe Browsing. No independent security audit, penetration test, bug bounty programme or disclosure policy was found in the pages consulted, and the contributor-binary warning is an explicit acknowledgement that supply-chain trust is not guaranteed outside distribution repositories.
content.update_channels_and_release_cadence: There is no ungoogled-chromium updater. Updates arrive either from a distribution package manager, from Flathub, or by rebuilding against a new tag, and the project's own cadence is expressed through those tags rather than through release announcements. Tags follow the form `{chromium_version}-{revision}`, where the version is the Chromium version the patches apply to and the revision counts ungoogled-chromium releases for that version; platform repositories extend the scheme. The most recent tags observed are `156.0.8078.73-1`, `156.0.8078.47-1` and `155.0.8059.84-1`, which shows two revisions of the same Chromium minor within weeks — the normal pattern for a project that must republish whenever Chromium ships a security update. The practical consequence is that the browser's security depends on how quickly a user's distribution rebuilds: a rolling distribution or Flathub tracks closely, a stale PPA does not, and a manually built binary is only as current as its builder. No beta or stable channels, no automatic update mechanism and no end-of-life policy for old tags are documented.
content.licensing_and_governance: ungoogled-chromium is licensed under the BSD 3-Clause licence, a choice that covers the project's own patches, scripts and utilities while the Chromium source it modifies remains under Chromium's own BSD-style licence and its many third-party components. Governance is a volunteer organisation rather than a company: the work happens in a GitHub organisation with one common repository and per-platform build repositories, code ownership is limited to a core team according to the repository's ownership file history, and a separate wiki carries the FAQ and design notes. Contribution rules are documented in a contributing guide that also sets criteria for accepting new features, and the project channels small or out-of-scope suggestions toward a contrib repository or the wiki instead of the main tree. The README explicitly asks for help and lists the issue tracker, especially the issues tagged as needing assistance, as the entry point. Forks are permitted and expected: the project lists downstream projects that borrow its patches, which is consistent with a permissively licensed patch set whose purpose is to be reused. No foundation, corporate sponsor or formal decision-making body is documented.
content.limitations_and_scope: The limitations follow directly from the design. There are no official binaries, so users depend on a distribution, Flathub, or contributor builds whose authenticity the project itself says cannot be guaranteed because they are not necessarily reproducible. There is no update mechanism inside the browser. Privacy features are largely opt-in: the project states that almost all of its enhancements must be manually activated, so a default install is close to Chromium with Google services removed rather than a hardened browser. Sites cannot sign in with Google accounts using FIDO U2F keys, as the FAQ documents, because the internal extension Google relies on is broken by the patches. Session data is discarded on close by default, which surprises users. Chrome Web Store installation requires workarounds, extension auto-update requires a third-party extension, and DRM requires manually transplanting Widevine from a matching Chrome build. Safe Browsing is absent, and the project's replacement advice is to install a content blocker. Beyond the project's own statements, no audit, no accessibility statement, no formal disclosure policy and no architecture matrix are published.
content.who_is_it_for: ungoogled-chromium is for users who want Chromium's engine, interface and extension model without its ties to Google's services, and who are willing to manage the consequences: install from a distribution or Flathub, keep it updated through that channel, and turn on the privacy switches they want. It suits administrators and packagers who value a patch set they can read, build and audit over a vendor binary, and it suits people on Linux distributions that already package it well, including OpenMandriva, where it is the default browser.
content.who_is_it_not_for: It is not for users who want a signed installer from a vendor, automatic updates, or a supported product with someone accountable at the other end. It is not for anyone who expects phishing and malware protection out of the box, since Safe Browsing is removed and no equivalent is bundled. It is not convenient for users who install many extensions from the Chrome Web Store, who rely on Google account sign-in with hardware security keys, or who want their browsing session to persist across restarts by default. And it is a poor fit for managed fleets, where the absence of reproducible official binaries, of a disclosure policy and of an update channel of its own makes it difficult to justify.
content.verdict: ungoogled-chromium is a patch set first and a browser second, and judging it as a product misses the point. As engineering, it is disciplined: a clear ordering of objectives, four documented mechanisms, a domain-substitution trick that makes residual Google requests visible rather than silent, and a refusal to bundle binaries it cannot vouch for. As a user experience, it is deliberately unfinished: no updater, no official artefact, most enhancements switched off, extension installation reduced to CRX plumbing, and Safe Browsing removed without replacement. It is the right choice for someone who wants stock Chromium with Google's services surgically removed and who has a package manager to keep it patched; it is the wrong choice for anyone who wants a finished, supported, self-updating browser.
